strengths: Combines the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) framework with a novel AGOP-guided binary tree partitioning scheme, giving a principled and reasonably scalable path (O(n log n) train, O(log n) inference) for feature-learning kernel machines on tabular data, which historically have not scaled or performed competitively.

Very extensive empirical evaluation across three benchmarks (TALENT with 300 datasets and 31 baselines, TabArena-Lite, and large meta-test datasets up to 500K samples), providing good coverage of dataset sizes and task types (regression, binary/multiclass classification).

Strong, clearly stated regression results: best aggregate performance among 31 methods on 100 TALENT regression datasets, and near/around Pareto frontier on TabArena-Lite in both accuracy and inference speed.

Interpretability is native to the method (via AGOP diagonal/eigenvectors) rather than requiring a separate post-hoc tool, and the paper provides intuitive, domain-plausible case studies (California housing, Covertype, NYC taxi, breast cancer) showing sensible and locally-varying feature importance across leaves.

Careful ablations/ improvements over the base kernel-RFM algorithm (generalized Lp,q kernels, diagonal vs. full AGOP, categorical variable speedups, adaptive bandwidth) with statistically significant improvement (Wilcoxon p<1e-4) over kernel ridge regression and standard RFM.
Reasonable transparency regarding hyperparameter search spaces, algorithmic pseudocode, and complexity analysis in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Classification results are only 'competitive' (often 3rd-5th place) rather than state-of-the-art, and on the fuller TabArena benchmark (Tables B.8-B.10) xRFM is solidly mid-pack (Elo ~1563 vs. top methods at ~1779), which is a more modest result than the framing in the abstract/intro might suggest to a casual reader.

Novelty is somewhat incremental/engineering-oriented: it combines an existing algorithm (RFM) with tree-based partitioning, a strategy already used in spirit by prior work (e.g., TabPFN-v2's random-forest-based sample routing), plus known kernel generalizations (Schoenberg kernels) and standard implementation optimizations.

Interpretability claims are validated only through a handful of hand-picked, qualitative case studies without systematic comparison to established interpretability baselines (e.g., SHAP, tree feature importances), despite the paper itself noting this comparison as important future work.

Comparison to TabPFN-v2 may be somewhat unfavorable to that baseline due to imposed constraints (subsampling to 10K, restriction to ≤10 classes), which could inflate xRFM's relative standing on some tasks without fully controlling for this.

Tables B.8 and B.10 (regression vs. binary classification results on TabArena) appear to contain identical numbers, suggesting a copy-paste error in the appendix that raises minor concerns about care taken in reporting full results.

Limited theoretical justification for why AGOP-based median-split partitioning is preferable to other (e.g., PCA/random projection) splitting strategies beyond an empirical claim; no formal guarantees are given for the O(n log n)/O(log n) complexity claims under non-ideal (imbalanced) splits.

The runtime plots (Fig. 5) show xRFM's cost scaling super-linearly below the leaf-size threshold, and the benefit of tree partitioning only manifests clearly above ~60K samples, limiting the significance of the scalability contribution for many practically-sized tabular datasets already well-served by GBDTs.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across three benchmarks (TALENT ~300 datasets, TabArena-Lite, and meta-test large datasets), which is a substantially broader evaluation than typical tabular ML papers.
Strong regression results: xRFM achieves best aggregate performance across all TALENT regression metrics and is on the Pareto frontier for accuracy vs. inference time in TabArena-Lite regression.
Clear algorithmic description with detailed pseudocode (Algorithms A.1-A.5) and hyperparameter search spaces provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.

Native interpretability via AGOP is a genuine practical advantage over black-box competitors like TabPFN-v2 and deep nets; the case studies (California housing, Covertype, Taxi tipping, Breast cancer) provide convincing, domain-sensible qualitative validation.

Good ablations isolating the contribution of the tree-partitioning component, including comparisons against standard kernel ridge regression and the original (non-tree) RFM with statistically significant improvements (Wilcoxon p<10^-4).
Favorable computational profile: fast inference (O(log n)) and competitive/superior training time compared to GBDTs and neural nets, especially on small-to-medium datasets.
weaknesses: Classification performance is only 'competitive' rather than best: xRFM ranks third or lower on multiple TALENT/TabArena classification splits, with TabPFN-v2, RealMLP, or ModernNCA often outperforming it, somewhat undercutting the broad claims in the abstract/intro.

The complexity/scalability story is partly oversold: Fig. 5 shows superlinear scaling until 60K samples, and the O(n log n) claim only holds asymptotically after the tree kicks in — this nuance could be stated more prominently rather than in a footnote.

Core novelty is somewhat incremental — it is largely a combination of existing components (RFM feature learning + tree-based recursive partitioning + generalized q,p kernels), each of which draws heavily on prior work; the conceptual leap beyond Radhakrishnan et al. (RFM) is limited to the partitioning scheme and minor kernel/bandwidth tuning tricks.

No ablation on the sensitivity of results to the leaf size hyperparameter C or the tree-splitting procedure itself (e.g., effect of using AGOP-derived splits vs. simpler heuristics is only qualitatively claimed as 'we found splitting in this manner outperformed... approaches' without quantitative support in the main results).

For the meta-test large-dataset comparisons, baseline numbers are taken from prior literature rather than re-run under an identical protocol/tuning budget, which weakens the fairness of direct comparison.

Reported inference/training times for xRFM are for the 'best hyperparameter configuration' only, while the paper explicitly notes TabPFN-v2 doesn't need this tuning overhead — implying the practical/total compute cost of xRFM (including HPO) may be considerably higher than reported per-configuration numbers suggest, and this overhead is not clearly quantified for xRFM itself.

The paper lacks a clear theoretical or empirical characterization of failure modes — e.g., on which types of tabular problems or data regimes xRFM underperforms GBDTs or TabPFN-v2, beyond aggregate benchmark rankings.
